newsitem.title: GERMANY: German coffee trade sees further nearby tightness.
newsitem.headline: German coffee trade sees further nearby tightness.

text.p: Green coffee markets in Germany will remain tight in early 1997 but roasters are mostly covered for the first quarter, coffee traders said on Monday.
"Differentials will stay firm regardless of futures falls to express that tightness," one said.
"But it doesn't have much impact because consumers are beginning to shut down operations for the Christmas and New Year holiday period and have therefore stopped buying."
New York arabica futures were pressurised by commission house selling last week and Hamburg traders thought weak technicals might encourage further falls after an initial bounce.
But they also believed origin selling would be moderate as producers were likely to try to safeguard reasonable returns, at least in the first quarter of 1997.
CSCE March closed at 103.25 cents/lb on Friday.

Physical coffee markets prepared for a holiday lull until mid-January, which traders said would only be shortened if ships were delayed at origin or if the winter turned out to be extremely cold. They believed both were unlikely.
The pace of roasted coffee sales, which usually peak at Christmas, did not appear extraordinary, they added.
On crop fundamentals, traders said they would ignore private sector estimates of Brazil's 1997/98 coffee harvest because it was much too early.
As in earlier years, warnings of a smaller crop at this stage would be interpreted as attempts to boost prices.
Arabicas in the Bremen import markets rose $1.50-2.00 per 50 kg fob on the week, with differentials rising.
Kenyans were at 50-60 cents over futures and Central Americans also above futures in a three to nine cents range.
Robusta buyers kept an eye on quality and transport problems arising from unusually heavy rainfall in Vietnam.
Colombia excelso was at $132, down $2, and Brazils at $106.00, off $1.50, while Indonesian robustas eased $2.00 to $59 December/January cif shipment.
